items.prompt: Per L1, what is "calibration"?
choices: A structured session where managers compare draft ratings against each other and a shared rubric before ratings are finalized
A single manager's private process of double-checking their own memory before writing a review
A tool that automatically assigns performance ratings based on ticket counts
The final step where HR announces raises, after all ratings are already locked
items.explanation: L1 defines calibration specifically as a cross-manager comparison against a shared rubric, before ratings are finalized — not a solo check or an automated process.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, are the manager's two individual reviews dishonest on their own?
choices: No — each review is honest in isolation; the unfairness comes from how unevenly the two periods of work were weighed
Yes — the manager fabricated details about the March launch
Yes — the manager deliberately punished the February engineer
The Scenario doesn't say whether the reviews were accurate
items.explanation: L1's closing question is explicit: both reviews are honest in isolation, yet they add up to something unfair — the problem is uneven weighing, not dishonesty.

items.prompt: What is "recency bias", as defined in L1?
choices: Weighing recent events more heavily than older ones when forming an overall judgment, regardless of which events actually mattered more
Preferring employees who were hired most recently over long-tenured ones
A rule that only the last quarter of the year counts toward a rating
A bias that only affects new managers, not experienced ones
items.explanation: L1 defines recency bias as weighing recent events more heavily regardless of their actual importance — it's about memory, not tenure or an explicit rule.

items.prompt: Why does the manager in the Scenario rate the March launch higher than the February fix?
choices: The March work is more recent and vivid in memory, while the February work has faded, even though both are real contributions
The March launch was objectively more valuable to the company
The February engineer asked not to be evaluated on that work
The manager was told to prioritize visible launches by policy
items.explanation: The Scenario is a case of recency bias specifically — vividness and recency drive the difference, not a genuine difference in value.

items.prompt: Per L1, what is the "halo effect"?
choices: Letting one strong, visible trait or result inflate the perceived quality of everything else about a person, including things not actually observed
The tendency for a manager to rate every report identically
A bonus given automatically to whoever ships the most visible project
The effect of a promotion making someone seem more senior than their actual scope
items.explanation: L1 defines the halo effect as one strong trait or result bleeding into judgments about unrelated, unobserved qualities.

items.prompt: Which of these would be an example of the halo effect during a review?
choices: Assuming someone's communication skills are excellent just because their code is excellent, without ever having observed their communication
Rating someone lower because they took a two-week vacation
Comparing two engineers using the same rubric
Asking a manager to cite a specific example before finalizing a rating
items.explanation: The halo effect is specifically about one observed strength bleeding into an unrelated, unobserved judgment — like inferring communication skill from code quality alone.

items.prompt: Per L1, what distinguishes "leniency bias" from "central-tendency bias"?
choices: Leniency is a manager's habit of rating generously overall; central tendency is clustering everyone near "meets expectations" to avoid hard conversations
Leniency only applies to junior employees; central tendency only applies to senior employees
They are the same thing with two different names
Leniency is about ratings being too low; central tendency is about ratings being too high
items.explanation: L1 distinguishes them as two related but distinct manager habits — generosity overall (leniency) versus avoiding extremes in either direction (central tendency).

items.prompt: What is a "calibration packet"?
choices: The written evidence — specific examples, dates, outcomes — a manager brings into a calibration session to support a proposed rating
The official HR form used to submit a final salary decision
A summary of a manager's entire team's headcount
A packet of feedback survey results collected from an employee's peers
items.explanation: L1 defines a calibration packet as the specific, dated evidence a manager brings to support a rating — not an HR form or a survey summary.

items.prompt: Per L2, why doesn't telling a manager to "just be objective" fix these biases?
choices: None of the biases feel like bias from the inside — a manager genuinely believes they're describing what happened, based on what they can recall
Managers are told to be objective, but choose not to be
Objectivity is impossible in any performance review, so there's no point trying
Bias only affects managers who have never received training
items.explanation: L2 makes the point that these biases are invisible from the inside — a manager isn't ignoring a call to be objective, they genuinely can't see the distortion in their own recall.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does calibration do instead of asking managers to "try harder" at being unbiased?
choices: It puts multiple managers' ratings side by side against a shared rubric, so a distortion invisible to one person becomes visible as an inconsistency between people
It removes managers from the review process entirely and lets HR decide
It asks each manager to rate their own bias on a scale of 1 to 5
It requires every employee to write their own performance review
items.explanation: L2's mechanism is comparison across managers and against a shared rubric — that's what surfaces a bias that's invisible to any one person alone.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what happens before the calibration session meeting?
choices: Each manager writes a draft rating and evidence packet independently, and these are shared across managers
The session happens first, then each manager writes up notes afterward
HR assigns final ratings, which managers can then appeal
Employees submit self-reviews that immediately become the final rating
items.explanation: L2's diagram is explicit about the order: independent drafts first, shared before the session, then the session itself.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does the independent-draft step matter — what would go wrong without it?
choices: Without committing to a rating and evidence before hearing others' opinions, the session surfaces less genuine disagreement, as people anchor to whoever spoke first
Without it, the session would take less time overall
Without it, managers wouldn't be allowed to disagree with each other at all
It doesn't actually matter — L2 says the order is arbitrary
items.explanation: L2 explains the independent-draft step specifically prevents anchoring to whoever speaks first, which is what lets genuine disagreement surface.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does calibration discussion start from evidence rather than from the rating number itself?
choices: "Do we agree this is a 4" invites a negotiation, while "what specific evidence supports a 4" invites a fact-check — which is what catches a thin, recency-biased packet
Starting with the rating number is against company policy in most organizations
Evidence-first discussion is faster, which is the only reason L2 gives
There is no real difference between the two approaches, per L2
items.explanation: L2 draws this distinction directly — evidence-first framing is what exposes a thin packet, while rating-first framing invites negotiating a number instead.

items.prompt: Per L2, why can't a calibration group use one single bar ("did great work") to compare a junior and a senior engineer?
choices: "Great work" means something different at each level — a single bar implicitly asks "who did more," which seniors will always win by default
Junior engineers are never allowed to be rated in the same session as senior engineers
A single bar is actually fine, and L2 recommends it for simplicity
Because junior and senior engineers work on entirely different teams
items.explanation: L2 explains a single undifferentiated bar collapses into "who did more," which structurally favors senior scope — a per-level rubric measures each person against what their own level requires.

items.prompt: Per L2's rubric table, what specifically distinguishes "meets expectations" for a senior engineer from a mid-level engineer?
choices: A senior identifies problems nobody assigned and unblocks others, not just themselves — a mid-level owns a feature end-to-end and scopes their own smaller tasks
A senior simply produces more code output than a mid-level engineer
A senior has more years of tenure at the company
There is no meaningful difference in L2's rubric — both are held to the same bar
items.explanation: L2's rubric table specifies scope of ownership per level — the senior bar is about unassigned problems and unblocking others, distinct from a mid-level's feature ownership.

items.prompt: In L3, what is missing from Dan's original draft packet for Sam, compared to Priya's packet for Wren?
choices: A specific, dated example with a concrete outcome — Dan's draft is a general impression with nothing cited
Dan's packet is missing a numeric rating entirely
Dan's packet accuses Sam of underperforming, which Priya's does not
Nothing is missing — both packets are equally detailed
items.explanation: L3 shows Dan's original draft as a general impression with no specific example, date, or outcome — exactly the gap calibration is designed to catch.

items.prompt: What did Sam actually do in February, per L3's worked example?
choices: Independently identified that a scheduled migration would corrupt production customer records, wrote and tested a fix, and prevented the incident
Shipped a customer-facing feature that increased conversion
Was assigned by a manager to audit the migration scripts
Reported a bug but did not personally fix it
items.explanation: L3 describes Sam independently catching and fixing an unassigned, high-risk migration bug — unassigned discovery is exactly what the senior rubric rewards.

items.prompt: Per L3, why did nobody outside the immediate team hear about Sam's February fix?
choices: Because Sam prevented the incident, nothing broke and no customer ever saw a symptom — so there was nothing visible to draw attention to it
Sam was explicitly told to keep it quiet by management
The fix was actually minor and not worth mentioning
Dan intentionally hid the incident from the rest of the company
items.explanation: L3 is explicit: because the fix prevented any visible symptom, there was nothing to draw attention to it — prevention is inherently less visible than a launch.

items.prompt: In L3's calibration session, whose packet does the group question first, and why?
choices: Dan's — the group starts with the thinnest packet, asking for specific evidence behind the draft rating
Priya's — the group starts by challenging the highest-rated packet on principle
Neither — both packets are accepted without discussion
The group starts with whichever manager has the most tenure
items.explanation: L3 shows the group deliberately starting with the thinnest, least-evidenced packet — consistent with L2's evidence-first mechanism.

items.prompt: Per L3's "extend it" section, what could an uncorrected draft rating for Sam actually cost, beyond "one review being slightly off"?
choices: If ratings feed a fixed distribution, Sam could lose a raise or promotion slot to someone else, and learn that quiet preventive work is worth less than visible launches
Nothing further — a single review has no downstream effect on pay or promotion
Sam would be immediately terminated as a result of the lower rating
The company would be legally required to disclose the error to Sam
items.explanation: L3 traces the real cost: a fixed rating distribution ties the error directly to pay/promotion outcomes and teaches the wrong lesson about what kind of work is valued.

items.prompt: What harder question does L3 raise about calibration across different teams?
choices: Whether one whole team's calibration group could be collectively lenient or harsh relative to another team's, even if each team's internal session went perfectly
Whether calibration should happen more than once per year
Whether managers should be allowed to calibrate their own direct reports
Whether calibration sessions should be recorded for legal purposes
items.explanation: L3's extension question is specifically about cross-team consistency — one group being collectively lenient or harsh relative to another, a second-order version of the same bias.

items.prompt: Per L3's closing failure modes, what is the risk of a fixed rating distribution (a set number of "4"s allowed per team)?
choices: It can reintroduce unfairness if two genuinely excellent people end up competing for one slot on the same team
It has no real risk — L3 recommends every team use one
It makes calibration sessions unnecessary, since ratings are decided in advance
It only affects junior employees, never senior ones
items.explanation: L3 flags that a fixed distribution is a pay-budget tool, not a claim about how performance is actually distributed — it can force two excellent people to compete for one slot.
